Digestive Upset.description: Gastrointestinal upset such as vomiting and/or diarrhea, commonly due to dietary indiscretion, infection, parasites, or systemic disease.
Digestive Upset.recommended_action: Offer small amounts of fresh water frequently. For healthy adult pets, withhold food for 8-12 hours, then reintroduce a bland diet in small portions. Do NOT fast young, very small, or chronically ill pets. Contact a veterinarian the same day if there are more than 2-3 episodes of vomiting or diarrhea, or if any blood, pain, or lethargy is noted.

Leg Injury.description: Lameness or leg pain that may be caused by soft tissue injury (sprain/strain), joint disease, or fracture.
Leg Injury.recommended_action: Restrict activity and prevent jumping or running. Confine to a small area if needed. You may apply a cold compress wrapped in a cloth for 5-10 minutes at a time if swelling is present. Do NOT give human pain medications. Arrange a veterinary examination within 24-48 hours, or sooner if pain is significant.

Respiratory Issue.description: Coughing, sneezing, or mild breathing changes that may be due to upper respiratory infection, allergies, or early respiratory disease.
Respiratory Issue.recommended_action: Monitor breathing rate and effort in a calm environment. Avoid stress, heat, and heavy exercise. If cough, sneezing, or nasal discharge persists longer than 2-3 days, or if appetite decreases, schedule a veterinary visit. Any sign of increased effort to breathe should be treated as urgent.

Skin Irritation.description: Itching, redness, or hair loss that may be related to allergies, parasites, skin infection, or contact irritation.
Skin Irritation.recommended_action: Check for fleas, ticks, or obvious skin lesions. Use an appropriate parasite control recommended for the species. Avoid bathing with harsh shampoos or applying human creams. If itching is persistent, the skin is worsening, or the pet is uncomfortable, schedule a veterinary visit for diagnosis and treatment.

Eye Problem.description: Eye discomfort or visible change that may be due to conjunctivitis, corneal ulcer, injury, or other ocular disease.
Eye Problem.recommended_action: Prevent the pet from rubbing or scratching the eye, and do not apply over-the-counter human eye drops. Keep the area around the eye gently clean with saline if needed. Because eye conditions can worsen quickly, a veterinary examination within 24 hours is recommended, sooner if pain appears significant.

Ear Problem.description: Ear discomfort that may be caused by infection, ear mites, foreign material, or allergic disease.
Ear Problem.recommended_action: Keep ears dry and avoid inserting cotton swabs or objects into the ear canal. Do not use home remedies or leftover medications without veterinary guidance. Schedule a veterinary visit for ear examination and appropriate cleaning and treatment, especially if symptoms last more than a few days.

Lethargy.description: Noticeable decrease in activity or responsiveness, which can be an early sign of many illnesses or pain.
Lethargy.recommended_action: Monitor closely for changes in appetite, drinking, urination, breathing, vomiting, or diarrhea. Ensure easy access to water and a quiet resting place. If lethargy lasts more than 24 hours, worsens, or occurs with other symptoms, contact a veterinarian the same day.

Loss of Appetite.description: Reduced or absent appetite, which may be associated with pain, fever, nausea, stress, or systemic disease.
Loss of Appetite.recommended_action: Offer a small amount of a familiar, palatable food and ensure fresh water is available. Do not force-feed or give human medications. If a normally healthy adult pet refuses all food for more than 24-48 hours, or sooner in young or chronically ill animals, contact a veterinarian for evaluation.

Excessive Drinking.description: Noticeable increase in drinking that can indicate hormonal disease, kidney problems, urinary tract disease, or other systemic issues.
Excessive Drinking.recommended_action: Measure or estimate daily water intake if possible and note urination frequency and volume. Do not restrict water. Schedule a veterinary visit for examination, blood tests, and urinalysis to identify underlying causes, especially if changes persist more than a few days.

Seizure.description: Sudden episode of abnormal brain activity causing involuntary movements, loss of awareness, or behavior changes.
Seizure.recommended_action: Do NOT restrain the pet. Move furniture and objects away to prevent injury and keep the area quiet and dark. Time the seizure if possible. Once the pet is safe and starting to recover, contact a veterinarian immediately, especially for first-time seizures, seizures lasting longer than 3-5 minutes, or more than one seizure in 24 hours.

Heatstroke / Heat Stress.description: Potential heat stress or heatstroke from high environmental temperatures or overexertion.
Heatstroke / Heat Stress.recommended_action: Move the pet to a cool shaded area immediately. Offer small amounts of cool (not ice-cold) water. Wet paws and belly with cool water and use a fan if available. Seek emergency veterinary care at once, especially if the pet is weak, collapsing, vomiting, or has bright red or pale gums.

Toxin Exposure / Possible Poisoning.description: Possible ingestion of a toxic substance such as food, plant, chemical, or human medication.
Toxin Exposure / Possible Poisoning.recommended_action: Contact a veterinarian or pet poison hotline immediately with the exact product name and amount eaten if known. Do not induce vomiting or give home remedies unless specifically instructed by a veterinarian. Bring the product packaging to the clinic if you go in.

Urinary Obstruction (Male Cat Emergency).description: Possible urethral blockage in a male cat. This is a true emergency and can be rapidly fatal without treatment.
Urinary Obstruction (Male Cat Emergency).recommended_action: This can be life-threatening. Seek emergency veterinary care immediately. Do not wait to see if it improves on its own. Do not give pain medications at home unless prescribed by a vet.

Urinary Issue.description: Possible urinary tract infection, bladder irritation, or other urinary tract issue.
Urinary Issue.recommended_action: Schedule a veterinary visit within 24 hours for examination and urine testing. Encourage water intake. Do not give over-the-counter human medications.

Bloat / Swollen Abdomen (Dog Emergency).description: Possible gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV) or other serious abdominal emergency, especially in large deep-chested dogs.
Bloat / Swollen Abdomen (Dog Emergency).recommended_action: This may be life-threatening. Go to an emergency veterinary hospital immediately. Do not wait at home or give food, water, or medications on your own.

Open Wound / Bleeding.description: Open wound, cut, or bite that may need cleaning, suturing, or antibiotics.
Open Wound / Bleeding.recommended_action: Apply gentle pressure with a clean cloth or bandage to control bleeding. Do not use hydrogen peroxide in deep wounds. See a veterinarian as soon as possible, especially for bite wounds or if bleeding does not stop within 5-10 minutes.

Allergic Reaction / Swelling.description: Possible allergic reaction, often after a sting, bite, new food, or medication.
Allergic Reaction / Swelling.recommended_action: If breathing is normal and the pet is comfortable, contact a veterinarian promptly for advice. If there is any trouble breathing, collapse, or vomiting, go to an emergency clinic immediately.

Pain / Vocalizing.description: General significant pain from injury, abdomen, back, or other causes.
Pain / Vocalizing.recommended_action: Minimize movement and keep the pet as calm and comfortable as possible. Do not give human pain medications as many are toxic to pets. Arrange a veterinary exam as soon as possible, same day if pain is significant.

Neurologic Issue / Hind Limb Weakness.description: Possible spinal, neurologic, or muscular problem affecting movement or coordination.
Neurologic Issue / Hind Limb Weakness.recommended_action: Restrict movement immediately and keep the pet confined to prevent further injury. Seek urgent veterinary evaluation the same day, especially if the pet cannot walk or control urination.

Acute Collapse / Not Responding.description: Sudden collapse or extreme weakness from many possible serious causes.
Acute Collapse / Not Responding.recommended_action: This is an emergency. Transport the pet to the nearest veterinary clinic or emergency hospital immediately. Keep the pet warm and quiet during transport. Call the clinic to let them know you are coming.

Dental / Mouth Problem.description: Dental disease or other oral pain that may affect eating and quality of life.
Dental / Mouth Problem.recommended_action: Schedule a veterinary dental check within the next 1-2 weeks. Offer softer food if chewing is difficult. Seek earlier care if the pet stops eating altogether or has facial swelling.

Gastrointestinal Foreign Body Suspected.description: Possible gastrointestinal foreign body that may cause obstruction.
Gastrointestinal Foreign Body Suspected.recommended_action: Contact a veterinarian promptly. Do not induce vomiting unless specifically instructed by a vet, especially if string, sharp objects, or unknown items are involved. Seek same-day examination if vomiting, lethargy, or loss of appetite develops.
